content: The studies included trials conducted in various countries: three in Australia, four in Brazil, one in the Caribbean Islands, one in Denmark and Sweden, three in France, one in China (Hong Kong SAR), eight in India, one in Ireland, four in Israel, four in Italy, one in Pakistan, one in Panama, two in South Africa, one in Sudan, two in Sweden, twelve in the United Kingdom, five in the United States, and one in Venezuela. Five trials recruited women admitted to hospitals, while another five included both inpatients and outpatients. Eighteen studies recruited women from hospital outpatient clinics, one from urban antenatal clinics, and three from antenatal clinics with unclear hospital affiliation. Seven studies recruited women in hospitals but did not specify the setting. Sixteen studies likely recruited women in hospital settings, while three had unclear settings. The trials were published between 1968 and 2017. The sample sizes of the trials were generally small, with 43 out of 58 trials including fewer than 130 women. The largest study included 314 participants. Four studies had three arms, while the rest had two arms. Only six studies had arms with more than 100 women. The gestational age at trial entry varied: 21 trials included only women in their third trimester, 20 included women in their second and third trimesters, eight included women in their first and second trimesters, and nine did not report gestational age at entry. In trials comparing antihypertensive drugs to placebo or no treatment, 11 trials recruited women before 32 weeks of gestation, two recruited women at 32 weeks or later, and 16 trials did not specify gestational age or disaggregate data by gestation. The severity of hypertension at trial entry varied due to differing inclusion criteria. Mild to moderate hypertension was defined with varying thresholds, with the lowest being 140 mmHg systolic and 85 mmHg diastolic. Five trials did not define thresholds for mild to moderate hypertension. Women with severe hypertension (systolic ≥170 mmHg or diastolic ≥110 mmHg) were excluded. Proteinuria at recruitment was reported variably: eight trials included only women with proteinuria, 19 excluded women with proteinuria, 14 included women regardless of proteinuria status, and 17 did not report proteinuria at entry. Ten trials included only women with chronic hypertension, 22 excluded women with chronic hypertension, 10 included women regardless of chronic hypertension status, and 16 did not mention chronic hypertension at entry. A variety of antihypertensive drugs and doses were used, all administered orally except for glyceryl trinitrate, which was given transdermally. Beta-blockers included acebutolol (400–1200 mg/day), atenolol (50–100 mg/day), labetalol (200–2500 mg/day in divided doses), mepindolol (5–10 mg/day), metoprolol (50–400 mg/day in one or two doses), oxprenolol (80–640 mg/day in one or two doses), pindolol (5–30 mg/day), and propranolol (30–160 mg/day). Alpha-agonists included methyldopa (250–8000 mg/day in one to four doses). Calcium channel blockers included amlodipine (5 mg/day), isradipine (10 mg/day in two doses), nicardipine (60 mg/day in three doses), nifedipine (20–160 mg/day, with one trial adjusting up to 30 mg/day as needed), nimodipine (120 mg/day in six-hourly doses), and verapamil (720 mg/day in three doses). Alpha-blockers included prazosin (3–15 mg/day in three doses). Nitric oxide donors included glyceryl trinitrate (10 mg/day). Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors included sildenafil (60–150 mg/day in three doses). Direct vasodilators included hydralazine (50–100 mg/day, with doses ranging from 50–300 mg in some trials, often combined with beta-blockers). Serotonin-2 receptor blockers included ketanserin (20–80 mg/day). Loop diuretics included furosemide (20 mg/day). The outcomes of pre-eclampsia and severe pre-eclampsia were defined differently across trials. Proteinuria/pre-eclampsia was generally defined as new proteinuria (≥1+ or ≥300 mg/24 hours), though some studies used higher thresholds (≥2+ or up to ≥5 g/24 hours). Some trials did not define pre-eclampsia criteria. Since the 2011 WHO recommendations on pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, the review has been updated twice (2014 and 2018), adding data from 12 trials (1627 women) and four antihypertensive drugs (oxprenolol, amlodipine, furosemide, and sildenafil). The 2011 recommendations included comparisons of any antihypertensive drug versus placebo/no drug, any drug versus methyldopa, and any drug versus calcium channel blockers. The 2018 update added a comparison of other antihypertensive drugs versus beta-blockers (19 trials). For maternal outcomes, it remains unclear whether antihypertensive drugs reduce maternal death, eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, or pulmonary edema due to very low-certainty evidence. Maternal death and severe maternal morbidity outcomes were rare or not reported. No trials reported on recurrent seizures, maternal ICU admissions, maternal satisfaction, or maternal well-being. For fetal/neonatal outcomes, the effects of antihypertensive drugs on perinatal death, neonatal bradycardia, or other adverse effects were unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. Beta-blockers versus placebo or no drug showed unclear effects on maternal death, eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, pulmonary edema, or placental abruption due to very low-certainty evidence. No trials reported on maternal ICU admissions, satisfaction, or well-being. The effects on perinatal death and neonatal bradycardia were also unclear. Methyldopa versus placebo or no drug showed unclear effects on maternal death, eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, proteinuria/pre-eclampsia, or placental abruption due to very low-certainty evidence. Adverse effects and fetal/neonatal outcomes, including perinatal death and NICU admission, were also unclear. Calcium channel blockers versus placebo or no drug showed unclear effects on eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, or placental abruption due to very low-certainty evidence. Maternal adverse effects and fetal/neonatal outcomes, including perinatal death and neonatal adverse effects, were also unclear. One small study compared prazosin to no drug, but the findings were unclear for all outcomes due to very low-certainty evidence. One study compared glyceryl trinitrate to no drug, reporting on proteinuria/pre-eclampsia, side effects, and drug discontinuation due to side effects, but the evidence was very low-certainty. The trial was stopped early due to side effects (headaches) in the treatment group. Two small studies compared sildenafil to placebo, but the effects on all outcomes were unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. No other comparisons of specific antihypertensive drugs versus placebo or no drug were reported. Beta-blockers compared to methyldopa showed unclear effects on severe pre-eclampsia, placental abruption, maternal side effects, drug discontinuation, neonatal hypoglycemia, bradycardia, or jaundice due to very low-certainty evidence. Calcium channel blockers compared to methyldopa showed unclear effects on eclampsia, proteinuria/pre-eclampsia, severe hypertension, maternal side effects, fetal/neonatal death, or NICU admission due to very low-certainty evidence. One small study compared ketanserin to methyldopa, reporting only on fetal/neonatal death, but the findings were unclear due to very low-certainty evidence. One small study compared glyceryl trinitrate to calcium channel blockers, but the findings were unclear.
